title: Where JavaScript Runs: Browser, Server and Other Runtime Environments
learningObjectives: Define a runtime environment as the execution context and host services available to a program.
Explain how JavaScript executes in browser engines and server-side runtimes.
Distinguish core ECMAScript features from APIs supplied by a host environment.
Identify browser APIs such as document, window, events, Fetch and localStorage.
Identify common server-side capabilities such as file access, process information and server networking.
Explain why browser code cannot assume that Node.js APIs are available and server code cannot assume a DOM exists.
Describe how a JavaScript engine and host runtime cooperate to execute code and provide services.
Explain the event loop at a conceptual level and identify timers, user events and network completions as sources of asynchronous work.
Recognize security differences between browser sandboxes and server processes with access to protected resources.
Compare common deployment contexts such as a browser page, a Node.js server, a serverless function and an edge runtime.
Choose environment-appropriate APIs and avoid exposing privileged server capabilities to client-side code.
Debug a runtime-specific error by identifying the environment and checking its available APIs.

understand.concept: JavaScript can run in several environments. In a browser, a JavaScript engine executes the language and the browser supplies Web APIs such as the DOM, events, Fetch and storage. In a server-side runtime such as Node.js, the engine is hosted with APIs for processes, files, networking and server applications. The core language is broadly shared, but the host APIs and security boundaries differ.
understand.whyItMatters: A common beginner error is to copy code from one JavaScript environment into another and assume its APIs exist. Identifying the runtime first helps you choose the right documentation, protect privileged operations and understand why a program works in one environment but fails in another.
understand.analogy: The language is like a common set of instructions; the runtime is the workplace that provides the tools and resources available to carry them out.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not show the technical security model. A browser page runs under browser sandbox and origin rules, while a server process may have access to files, secrets and network services according to its permissions.
understand.history: JavaScript began in browsers, but independent engines and server-side runtimes expanded where it could be used. Modern JavaScript tooling also runs in command-line and build environments. The language is shared, while the host environment determines which APIs are available.

explain.narrative:
The JavaScript language describes syntax and core behaviour, but it does not provide every capability an application needs. A runtime executes the code and supplies host APIs. In a browser, document.querySelector() accesses the page's DOM, addEventListener() responds to events, fetch() can request resources and localStorage can store origin-scoped data. These are Web platform APIs.

In Node.js, code commonly uses process information, file-system APIs, server networking and package modules. A Node.js process does not automatically have a document or window because it is not running inside a browser page. Other runtimes, such as serverless and edge environments, provide their own combinations of APIs and restrictions.

The engine and runtime work together. The engine evaluates JavaScript, while the host environment schedules events and exposes services. Asynchronous operations such as timers and network requests complete later and schedule callbacks or promise continuations. The event loop coordinates when this work can run. A program that assumes a network response arrives immediately or that an event handler runs synchronously can contain race conditions.

Security boundaries differ. Browser code is delivered to a user's device and can be inspected or modified; it must not contain privileged credentials. Server code can access protected resources, but only according to its identity and permissions. Validate and authorize operations on the server. Do not expose file-system or secret-management capabilities to untrusted browser code.

Before using an API, identify the runtime and consult its documentation. If an error says document is not defined, ask whether the code is running outside a browser. If process is unavailable, check whether the code is actually running in Node.js or a restricted browser/edge runtime.

examples.explanation: This example depends on the browser DOM. A server-side JavaScript program would use different APIs to produce output.
examples.expectedOutput: A browser page displays or updates text using JavaScript.

examples.title: Browser JavaScript uses Web APIs
examples.explanation: document is provided by the browser DOM environment. This code expects a page and will not work unchanged in a basic server runtime without a DOM implementation.
examples.expectedOutput: The page heading changes when the code runs in a browser.

examples.title: Server-side JavaScript uses runtime APIs
examples.explanation: The node:fs/promises module is a Node.js API. It is not a browser DOM feature and should not be imported into ordinary client-side code.
examples.expectedOutput: The program reads a local file when run in a permitted Node.js environment.

examples.title: Choose APIs according to the host
examples.code:
Browser host: document, window, DOM events, localStorage
Node.js host: process, file system, server networking
Edge host: request/response APIs and runtime-specific limits
Core language: variables, functions, objects, promises, modules
examples.explanation: The host environment determines available APIs and permissions. A runtime-specific program should document and test its environment assumptions.
examples.expectedOutput: You can classify an API by the runtime that supplies it.

practise.guidedTask: Take one browser JavaScript example and identify every API it uses. Then explain which parts are core ECMAScript and which parts require a browser. Compare it with a simple Node.js file-reading example and list the runtime assumptions.
practise.independentTask: Design a small application split into browser and server responsibilities. List which code runs in each runtime, which APIs each side can use, what data crosses the network and where authentication, authorization and secrets are handled.
hints: The runtime supplies host APIs; ECMAScript defines the core language.
document and window are browser APIs, not universal JavaScript globals.
Node.js provides file and process APIs but does not automatically provide a page DOM.
Server-side code must protect secrets and enforce authorization.
Asynchronous network and timer work completes later through the runtime's scheduling model.

practice.starterCode:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"><title>Where JavaScript runs: browser and server runtimes</title></head><body>
<script>const message='Browser runtime';document.body.insertAdjacentText('beforeend',message);</script>
</body></html>

questions.prompt: Which API is specific to browser documents and not available by default in Node.js?
questions.explanation: document is a browser DOM API and is not a built-in global in a standard Node.js process.

questions.prompt: What should you identify before using a JavaScript API?
questions.explanation: Available APIs depend on whether code runs in a browser, server runtime, or another host.

questions.prompt: Why does document.querySelector fail in a basic Node.js process?
options: The Node.js environment does not automatically provide a browser DOM.
The document object is part of CSS.
questions.answer: The Node.js environment does not automatically provide a browser DOM.
questions.explanation: document is a browser Web API. A server runtime does not automatically include the DOM.

questions.prompt: Which capability is commonly provided by Node.js rather than the browser page environment?
options: Access to the server process and file-system APIs, subject to permissions
questions.answer: Access to the server process and file-system APIs, subject to permissions
questions.explanation: Node.js exposes server/runtime APIs that are not generally available to ordinary browser page scripts.

questions.prompt: What should you identify before selecting a JavaScript API?
questions.explanation: Available APIs depend on whether the code runs in a browser, server runtime or another host.
